caption: Categories of Software Requirements
description: Classification of software requirements and the relationships among the categories. Software Requirements split into Software Project Requirements and Software Product Requirements. Software Product Requirements are further divided into Functional Requirements and Nonfunctional Requirements; Nonfunctional Requirements are subdivided into Technology Constraints and Quality of Service Constraints.

caption: Software Requirements Activities
description: The requirements activities. Requirements work comprises Requirements Development — reaching agreement on what software is to be constructed, consisting of Elicitation, Analysis, Specification and Validation — and Requirements Management — maintaining that agreement over time, consisting of Scrubbing, Change Control and Scope Matching.

caption: Value as a Function of Level of Performance
description: A plot of Value (vertical axis) against Level of Performance (horizontal axis), with no numeric scale — it shows a relationship, not data. The value curve is S-shaped: it stays low and nearly flat at low performance, rises steeply as performance increases, then levels off into a plateau at high performance. Two points are marked on the curve. The "Fail" point is at the lower knee: the least-favourable performance level, below which reducing performance further yields essentially no further loss of value. The "Perfection" point is at the upper knee: the most-favourable level, beyond which higher performance adds essentially no further value. This depicts a quality-of-service constraint whose value increases with performance (e.g., capacity, throughput, reliability); for constraints whose value decreases as performance increases (e.g., response time, mean time to repair), the same curve is mirrored.

caption: Most Cost-Effective Level of Performance
description: A plot of two quantities measured in money ($, vertical axis) against Level of Performance (horizontal axis), with no numeric scale. One curve is Value: an S-shape that is low at low performance, rises steeply in the middle, and plateaus at high performance (the same shape as Figure 1.4). The other curve is Cost to deliver: a rising step function — cost stays flat, then jumps up to a higher level, then jumps again — because each increment of achievable performance requires a discrete jump in investment. The marked "most cost-effective level of performance" is the point on the horizontal axis where the vertical distance between Value and Cost (value minus cost) is greatest, i.e., where net benefit is maximised.

caption: Example of Structured Natural Language Specification for a Single Use Case
description:
An example of a structured natural language requirements specification for a
single use case (use case #66, "Reserve flight(s)"). The template captures
the following fields:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Use case name | Reserve flight(s) |
| Triggering event(s) | Customer requests reservation(s) on flight(s) |
| Parameters | Passenger, itinerary, fare class, payment method(s) |
| Requires | Legal itinerary, fare class restrictions met |
| Guarantees | Seat(s) reserved for passenger on itinerary flight(s) |
| Normal course | Non-FF passenger, all domestic itinerary, Economy fare class, credit/debit card |
| Alternative course(s) | FF passenger [None, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Elite]; Itinerary [all international, mixed domestic + international]; Fare class [Basic economy, Premium Economy, Business, First]; Payment method [Voucher, FF miles] |
| Exceptions | C/D card declined, voucher doesn't exist, voucher expired, FF account doesn't exist, insufficient miles in FF account |
